section_summary: This section opens with a Board of Economic Warfare letter and four March 1943 assessments of Japan’s wartime supplies of cobalt, mercury, vanadium, and molybdenum. It then contains a Montevideo Embassy despatch and Military Attaché report based on Soviet diplomatic couriers’ observations of food shortages, surveillance, transportation, and military conditions in Japan and its empire. The remainder begins a translated Chinese study of Japan’s economic motives, Greater East Asia administrative machinery, puppet governments, resource exploitation, pacification campaigns, and collaborationist civic organizations; that report continues beyond page 40.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting studies of Japan’s strategic-material position
subfiles.from: John Fischer, Office of Economic Warfare Analysis
subfiles.to: Thomas K. Finletter, Special Assistant to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits assessments of Japan’s supplies of mercury, molybdenum, cobalt, and vanadium, together with a survey of Japanese aluminum developments.
subfiles.summary: Fischer tells Finletter that the enclosed mineral-supply summaries may be of interest. He also identifies an enclosed survey of Japanese aluminum developments since October 1942, although that survey is not included in this section. State Department receipt markings date from April 1943, but the letter itself has no visible date line.

subfiles.title: Cobalt: Summary of Japan’s Supply Position
subfiles.from: Board of Economic Warfare, Enemy Branch
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s 1943 cobalt supply, requirements, sources, uses, substitutes, and prospective stocks.
subfiles.summary: The report judges that Japan can meet minimum cobalt requirements if it retains the Bawdwin Mine and could expand use or accumulate stocks if maximum production is reached. It estimates 116–266 metric tons of new supply against requirements of at least 100 tons, with Burma providing nearly all prospective output. Notes discuss U.S. consumption patterns, essential military applications, substitutes, recovery factors, and uncertainty over Bawdwin production.

subfiles.title: Mercury: Summary of Japan’s Supply Position
subfiles.from: Board of Economic Warfare, Enemy Branch
subfiles.about: Evaluates Japan’s mercury stocks, current requirements, possible foreign supplies, and principal industrial uses.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Japan’s apparent mercury position as strong but notes strenuous efforts to obtain more, possibly because industrial expansion and the Honshu–Kyushu tunnel required large capital installations. Estimated opening stocks are 1,400 metric tons, with new supplies ranging from 21 to roughly 500 tons and annual requirements estimated at 500 tons. Possible additional mercury could be smuggled from Italy, Spain, or Free China, while deposits in Manchuria and North Borneo are also discussed.

subfiles.title: Vanadium: Summary of Japan’s Supply Position
subfiles.from: Board of Economic Warfare, Enemy Branch
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s vanadium production capacity, requirements, reserves, applications, and substitutes.
subfiles.summary: The report concludes that Japan’s vanadium position could be secure indefinitely if even half of its claimed extraction capacity from metallic sands and ores was effective. It estimates 650 tons in opening stocks, 420 tons of new supply, and requirements of about 200 tons, leaving 870 tons at the start of 1944. Most new output is assigned to Japan proper, while Manchuria is credited with a small and uncertain amount; tungsten and molybdenum are identified as possible substitutes.

subfiles.title: Molybdenum: Summary of Japan’s Supply Position
subfiles.from: Board of Economic Warfare, Enemy Branch
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s molybdenum reserves, production sources, wartime consumption, and substitute ferroalloys.
subfiles.summary: The report states that Japan’s molybdenum position should be secure for eight to ten years unless requirements have been seriously underestimated. It estimates stocks of 2,460 tons, 150 tons of new 1943 supply, and annual requirements of 400 tons, with Korea supplying most new production and smaller amounts coming from Manchuria and occupied China. Large Japanese tungsten supplies are said to reduce the need for molybdenum, while deposits in Zhejiang and Jiangxi may provide additional output.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4542: Japanese Financial and Economic Conditions
subfiles.from: Dudley G. Dwyre for the U.S. Ambassador, Montevideo
subfiles.about: Forwards a Military Attaché report of conversations with two Soviet diplomatic couriers recently returned from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy responds to the Department’s April 21 request for information from local residents concerning economic and financial conditions in the Japanese Empire. It encloses a Military Attaché report summarizing statements by two Soviet diplomatic couriers who had recently traveled through Japan and its occupied territories.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 2759 on Two Soviet Diplomatic Couriers
subfiles.from: Norman A. Congdon and William A. Tidwell, Office of the Military Attaché, Uruguay
subfiles.about: Records Soviet diplomatic couriers’ observations from recent journeys through Japan, Korea, and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The couriers reported constant Japanese police surveillance, serious shortages of meat, sugar, and bread, and fear of maritime travel because ships were being sunk. They saw few troops in Japan proper and heard that many forces and air bases were concentrated in Korea and Manchuria for operations against China. They emphasized the effects of the Allied submarine campaign and suggested that Soviet help against Japan might follow Hitler’s defeat, but language difficulties limited the interview.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2774 transmitting “The Political and Economic Aspects of Japan’s Puppet Organizations”
subfiles.about: Transmits a single FEA translation of Li Chow-ying’s report on Japan’s puppet political and economic organizations.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy forwards one copy of a translation prepared by FEA in Chungking of a report by Li Chow-ying, director of the Kuomintang Economic Service. Because of its length, the Embassy made no additional copies and retained none in its files. The local FEA office had separately sent copies to FEA in Washington on July 13, 1944.

subfiles.title: The Political and Economic Aspects of Japan’s Puppet Organizations
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s motives, institutions, economic programs, puppet regimes, pacification machinery, and civic organizations in occupied China.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that Japan’s aggression was driven by the need for raw materials, food, and additional industrial capacity, and describes the Asia Office, Ministry of Greater East Asia, planning councils, and development corporations used to direct expansion. It traces successive policies for a Japan–Manchuria–China economic bloc and Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, emphasizing resource seizure, compulsory purchasing, rationing, blockade, and the use of puppet governments. It then surveys Manchukuo, Mongolian, North China, and Nanjing regimes and the tensions between Japanese control and Wang Jingwei’s claims to political and economic authority. The final pages in this section describe North and Central China pacification campaigns, taxation and grain seizures, blockade systems, police and intelligence machinery, and collaborationist civic groups before beginning a discussion of puppet educational policy.
